question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?

forecasts.reference-class: UK immigration policy proposals in 2025–2026 to raise the settlement qualifying period from 5 years to 10 years for most routes (the 'earned settlement' baseline), currently under public consultation with responses through February 2026; policy not yet enacted as of March 2026.

sources.claim: House of Commons Library briefing describing the government’s 2025 proposal to set a ten-year baseline qualifying period for most settlement routes, with exemptions based on circumstances.
Explanatory memorandum accompanying the 2025 immigration rule changes; discusses settlement reforms and related private-life provisions.
Migration Observatory analysis noting longer residency requirements and public consultation through February 2026.
House of Commons Library briefing on petitions opposing the 10-year ILR proposal and noting the government’s position that a decision has not yet been taken; consultation ongoing.
GOV.UK guidance showing the 10-year long residence route as an existing pathway to settlement.
GOV.UK continuous-residence guidance detailing qualifying periods and the counting of time toward settlement across routes.
The plan states the route to settlement will extend from five to 10 years, with reductions for those who contribute to the economy.

The Home Secretary announced a proposed new contribution-based settlement model requiring a minimum of 10 years of lawful residence, double the current period, with a consultation to be launched by the end of the year.
House of Commons Library states a ten-year baseline for permanent residence (ILR) with some people able to qualify sooner based on criteria to be decided following public consultation.
Earlier in 2025 the government announced doubling the permanent settlement qualifying period for migrants to 10 years.
BBC reports Labour's Immigration White Paper plans extend the pathway to citizenship to a decade, i.e., 10 years before settlement.
Guardian reports the white paper proposes extending the settlement wait to 10 years for many migrants.

The government announced details in November 2025 proposing a 10-year baseline qualifying period for ILR, with some routes potentially qualifying sooner; a consultation ran through February 2026 and changes could be implemented from April 2026 if adopted.
The proposal introduces 'Earned Settlement' and a baseline 10-year ILR path; a 12-week consultation ended in February 2026; implementation could occur from April 2026 if the reforms are enacted.
The government signaled extending the settlement waiting period from five to ten years in a 2025 immigration white paper, with consultation ongoing and potential policy changes.
IPPR warns that hundreds of thousands of children could face a 10-year settlement wait under proposed changes, highlighting the potential scale and timing of reform in 2026.

causal-factors.name: Ten-year baseline for settlement (Earned settlement framework)
causal-factors.rationale: The government’s November 2025 Earned Settlement consultation explicitly proposes a 10-year baseline for most settlement routes, with potential implementation starting as early as April 2026, creating strong momentum toward a 10-year threshold by May 2026. (sources: GOV.UK Earned settlement [turn1view0], A Fairer Pathway to Settlement accessible [turn2view0], Commons Library cbp-10267 [turn5search1])

causal-factors.name: Imminent implementation window following February 2026 consultation
causal-factors.rationale: Public materials indicate the consultation closed in mid-February 2026 and that rules could begin changing from April 2026, tightening the timeline and increasing the odds changes are in force by May 2026. (sources: GOV.UK Earned settlement [turn1view0], A Fairer Pathway to Settlement accessible [turn2view0])

causal-factors.name: Fairness concerns and potential legal/political pushback
causal-factors.rationale: Think-tank and media coverage warn about the fairness of retroactive changes and large impacts on families and children, raising the risk of delays, modifications, or legal challenges to the proposed model. (sources: Guardian IPPR analysis [turn0search2], Guardian coverage on fairness concerns [turn5search6], FT coverage of policy risks [turn5news14])

causal-factors.name: Exemption and time-adjustment provisions (not universal 10-year wait)
causal-factors.rationale: The earned settlement framework includes exemptions and a time-adjustment mechanism that can shorten or lengthen the baseline for individuals based on contributions, meaning the 10-year default would not apply uniformly. (sources: GOV.UK accessible consultation text [turn2view0], Commons Library material on exemptions [turn4search0])

causal-factors.name: Policy momentum from official announcements and parliamentary coverage
causal-factors.rationale: Multiple official and parliamentary briefings describe a move toward a 10-year ILR/settlement pathway, with discussion ongoing in late 2025 and early 2026; this raises the probability of a 10-year threshold being adopted by May 2026. (sources: Hansard migration settlement debate [turn4search2], Commons Library briefing cbp-10267 [turn5search1])

causal-factors.name: Possibility of transitional arrangements/exemptions delaying enactment
causal-factors.rationale: Consultation materials envisage transitional rules and exemptions, which could slow or limit immediate implementation by May 2026. causal-factors.rationale: Extensive media coverage and policy discourse (BBC/Guardian reporting and IPPR commentary) reinforce the reform trajectory toward longer settlement waits, supporting the probability of changes by May 2026, though with caveats. synthesis: The ensemble suggests modest probability of a 10-year settlement threshold by May 2026, but substantive objections about enactment timing and transitional rules imply a downward risk. Calibrated probability centers around 52%, reflecting momentum with notable uncertainty.
